policy_title: Reverse Conservative Bank Tax Cuts and Impose Windfall Tax on Energy Companies
stated: Reverse Conservative tax cuts for big banks by restoring Bank Surcharge and Bank Levy revenues to 2016 levels in real terms, and introduce a proper, one-off windfall tax on the super-profits of oil and gas producers and traders.

source.quote: Implement a tax policy that recognises how high the Conservatives have raised personal taxes, making the cost-of-living crisis worse, by instead focusing tax changes on reversing the Conservatives’ tax cuts for big banks and imposing a proper, one-off windfall tax on the super-profits of oil and gas producers and traders.

bearing_set.reason: The windfall tax on oil and gas producers directly intersects with the energy market that determines household energy bills (a core O2 indicator); restoring bank surcharge/levy revenues could also affect consumer credit and borrowing costs, though this pass-through is more contested.

Restoring bank levy/surcharge to 2016 real-term levels and imposing a windfall tax materially raises tax revenue, directly improving the funded/borrowed balance and bearing on public-finance sustainability.

Bank and oil/gas super-profits accrue disproportionately to wealthy shareholders; taxing them narrows the post-tax income/wealth gap via a concrete distributional mechanism affecting Gini and top-decile income shares.

A permanent rise in bank-sector taxes could reduce lending capacity or credit availability, and a windfall tax (even one-off) sets a precedent that may dampen energy-sector investment — concrete mechanisms that bear on business investment and productivity indicators.

membership_note: The policy operates on corporate rather than household tax, so O11 (take-home pay) is not directly in scope. O2 pass-through effects are too indirect for a one-off windfall tax to clear the non-negligible bar. The three bearings above cover the fiscal gain (O12), distributional shift (O14), and the contested investment/growth tradeoff (O13).
